assumptions: The parents' installer provides only voluntary workflow discovery or a separately contracted pilot and confers no automatic customer, technician, data, warranty, or commercial rights.
All dispatched work would be limited to jobs for which the operating entity and assigned technician hold the required electrical, F-gas, OEM, insurance, and data-processing permissions.
The stated prices, margins, subscription count, and founder-wealth path are hypotheses rather than validated forecasts.

Unknown demand, conversion, retention, and operating metrics are treated as uncertainty rather than as proof of failure, while direct competitor, regulatory, labor, and price evidence is treated as structurally informative.
The founder remains in full-time employment, contributes no more than five hours per day, and must delegate live dispatch and escalation before meaningful scale.
No evidence beyond the scoped candidate and research packet is assumed.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: A bounded paid pilot with unrelated parties should pair at least one signed, priced technician-capacity commitment with installer prepayment and report incident density, remote-resolution share, response compliance, travel, first-visit resolution, rework and credits, fully loaded contribution margin, acquisition effort, renewal intent, and the exact OEM, qualification, insurance, and data rights for every job type.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: The concept correctly identifies a mismatch between installers' intermittent but deadline-sensitive callback burden and the cost of staffing permanent spare field capacity. Pre-reserving local technician time is a coherent response, but the packet does not establish that reservation is superior to spot dispatch, remote triage, or OEM service networks.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: Consumer-remedy obligations and Panasonic's service deadlines show that callbacks can impose urgent, measurable costs on installers. That supports genuine pain, but no unrelated installer has prepaid, signed an LOI, or accepted the proposed 900-2500 PLN monthly reservation plus dispatch margin, and remote resolution may reduce paid field events.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: Advance reservation billing could improve cash conversion, but the model carries utilization, travel, rework, standby-capacity, dispatcher, liability, and correlated-peak risk. Observed retail service pricing does not demonstrate room for the proposed 250-600 PLN routing margin, while incident frequency, CAC, retention, technician reservation cost, and fully loaded contribution economics are all unknown.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: Poland's roughly 1.5 million prosumer microinstallations and regional DSO concentration indicate a substantial installed-service surface. However, the addressable overflow-reservation market is not sized, postcode-level incident and route density are unknown, and combining PV, batteries, and heat pumps makes the initial beachhead less operationally narrow than it appears.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: CS-OZE already offers Polish installers outsourced aftercare while preserving their commercial relationship and recruits local technicians on flexible terms. OEM-authorized networks and direct-to-owner services add further alternatives, while the candidate controls neither essential service rights nor an exclusive supply base, leaving little present basis for regional domination.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: A working single-zone operation could extend into adjacent postcodes, installer portfolios, monitoring, inspections, batteries, and heat pumps. Each expansion, however, adds qualification, OEM authorization, parts, data-access, routing, and support complexity, so replication is not yet demonstrated to have attractive operating leverage.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: Nonexclusive, replaceable technician reservations are readily imitable and revocable, and incumbent networks can bundle similar coverage. Dispatch and fault data might eventually improve operations, but the packet does not establish permissioned proprietary access, data uniqueness, switching costs, or a compounding advantage unavailable to OEMs and existing service networks.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: Guaranteed local response windows could outperform ad hoc subcontracting during peaks, and retaining the installer's end-customer relationship addresses a trust objection. The advantage remains hypothetical: CS-OZE addresses the same workflow with lower technician commitment, and no evidence shows that reserved blocks deliver enough reliability or first-visit resolution to justify their fixed cost.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: A large aging installed base, enforceable service obligations, and shortages in qualified electrical and energy labor create timely pressure for aftercare capacity. The same labor shortage raises supply cost and refusal risk, while remote resolution and OEM-controlled service ecosystems weaken the case that this particular capacity-reservation structure is the timely winner.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: The founder has a lawful opt-in family-firm route to learn and pilot, while public installer registers, wholesalers, and technician referrals provide identifiable channels. Still, the model requires trust-heavy B2B selling on both sides, has no evidence of unrelated-customer conversion or CAC payback, and must overcome an incumbent already addressing the same buyer concern.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: The initial capital estimate fits the founder's stated resources and quantitative routing work fits his skills, but delivery is a safety- and liability-sensitive field operation. Job-level electrical, F-gas, and OEM permissions fragment supply; live triage and escalation threaten the five-hour daily limit; and scarce capacity may fail precisely during correlated regional peaks.

highest_value_structural_change: Narrow the business to one service category, one OEM-compatible authorization set, and one dense zone, aggregate paid installer demand before buying capacity, and sell an outcome-based resolution SLA with remote triage rather than a broad multi-brand reservation promise. This is a proposed change, not an evidenced redesign of v1.
main_structural_strength: The offer turns an intermittent operational liability into a measurable outsourced SLA while contractually leaving the end-customer relationship with the installer; if demand density and supply commitments clear at workable prices, that can be more useful than either permanent spare staffing or unstructured subcontracting.
primary_score_limiter: The core two-sided economics are unproven: there is no observed price at which qualified, appropriately authorized technicians will commit enforceable standby capacity and unrelated installers will prepay enough to cover utilization, travel, failure, support, and liability costs while leaving attractive owner earnings.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: CS-OZE already markets a close Polish substitute to the same installer buyer, preserves the installer's customer relationship, and sources nearby technicians through a nonexclusive, technician-choice model. This directly challenges both differentiation and the claim that prepaid reserved blocks are necessary to coordinate supply.
